dok_rationale: Part (c) asks the student to adjudicate two students' classifications of number-coded variables, justify each with the definition, and predict what specific calculation becomes meaningless under the wrong choice; both classifications of the rating can be defended, so the reasoning, not the label, is what is scored.
stem: A school newspaper surveyed six students for a story about getting to school. The table records lunch period, ZIP code, commute time in minutes, and a 1--5-star opinion rating of the commute.\par\smallskip Two reporters disagree about the numbers in it. \textbf{Maya:} ``Zip code and Rating are both quantitative --- they're numbers, so we can average them.'' \textbf{Jordan:} ``They're both categorical. Numbers can be labels.''
first_take: Would averaging two ZIP codes tell a reader anything useful about getting to school? Give one reason.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Who are the individuals in this data set?

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Classify Lunch, ZIP, and Min as categorical or quantitative. Give the unit for Min.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Decide whose ZIP-code claim is right and explain why an average ZIP code would or would not be meaningful. Then defend a classification for the star rating using what the numbers represent.

answers.a: The six surveyed students are the individuals.
answers.b: Lunch and ZIP are categorical labels; Min is quantitative commute time, measured in minutes.
answers.c: Jordan is right about ZIP: the digits label places, not measured or counted quantities. Averaging 01902 and 01905 gives 01903.5, which does not describe an average commute or location. The star rating is categorical when its numbers label ordered opinions. Accept a quantitative interpretation only if the student explicitly assumes equal steps on a measured score scale; writing `stars' alone is not enough.

expectedElements.description: Supports Jordan on ZIP and distinguishes location labels from quantities
Explains what an average ZIP code fails to measure or describe
Defends rating as opinion labels, or explicitly assumes an equal-step measured score

scoringGuide.E: All three elements are correct and linked to this problem. Accept equivalent plain-language reasoning.
scoringGuide.P: At least one element includes a correct evidence-to-reason link, but another is missing or incorrect.
scoringGuide.I: No correct evidence-to-reason link; only a choice, copied numbers, or unsupported statements.

commonMistakes: `It has digits, so it's quantitative' --- confuses how a value is written with what it measures
Saying zip code is categorical `because you can't add them' without saying WHY (it measures/counts nothing)
Treating Rating as obviously quantitative because the quiz app computes an average star rating
Naming the individuals as `the newspaper' or `the school' instead of the six students

sentence_frames: I agree with \blank[0.8in] about ZIP because those numbers represent \blank[1.8in]. An average would not tell us \blank[1.8in].
I treat the star rating as \blank[1in] because I assume the numbers mean \blank[2in].

dok_rationale: Classifying four described variables and supplying a unit for each quantitative one applies the definition across cases in one known procedure.
stem: For each variable, write \textbf{C} (categorical) or \textbf{Q} (quantitative); for each Q, give the unit: (1) jersey number of a soccer player; (2) number of goals scored this season; (3) shoe size; (4) preferred position (goalkeeper, defender, midfielder, forward); (5) minutes played in the last match.

answers.a: (1) C --- a label, even though numeric. (2) Q, goals. (3) Q, shoe-size units (a measured foot length on a scale); accept C with a reason that sizes are ordered labels. (4) C. (5) Q, minutes.
